name: Paradigm Shift
statement: Science advances not by steady accumulation but by revolutions that overturn one worldview for another.
statementAccent: revolutions that overturn one worldview for another
meaning: A paradigm shift is a fundamental change in the basic concepts, assumptions, methods, and practices of a scientific discipline, in which one paradigm is superseded by a rival, as described by Thomas Kuhn in his landmark 1962 book The Structure of Scientific Revolutions. At the center of Kuhn's account is the notion of a paradigm, a shared framework of theories, methods, standards, and exemplary problem-solutions that defines a scientific community and guides its work. The term is famously ambiguous, and the critic Margaret Masterman identified at least twenty-one different senses of it in Kuhn's book; Kuhn later distinguished the broad disciplinary matrix, the whole constellation of shared commitments, from the narrow exemplar, the concrete model solutions that train practitioners. Within an accepted paradigm, scientists do normal science, the routine puzzle-solving that articulates and extends the paradigm without testing its foundations. Over time, normal science turns up anomalies, results the paradigm cannot accommodate; when these accumulate and grow serious, the field enters crisis, and a scientific revolution may follow in which a new paradigm replaces the old, a paradigm shift. Kuhn argued that rival paradigms are incommensurable, lacking a fully neutral common measure, so the choice between them is not dictated by evidence and logic alone. His examples include the Copernican, Newtonian-to-Einsteinian, and chemical revolutions.
mechanism: Kuhn's model describes a cycle through which sciences develop and occasionally transform. A mature science operates under a reigning paradigm that supplies its accepted theories, its standards of good work, its instruments, and, crucially, its exemplars, the concrete achievements that show practitioners how problems are to be solved. Under this paradigm scientists conduct normal science, treating the framework itself as settled and devoting themselves to puzzle-solving: extending the paradigm's reach, measuring constants more precisely, and reconciling apparent discrepancies. Normal science is not aimed at testing or overthrowing the paradigm, and its very success in defining sharp puzzles brings anomalies into focus, findings that stubbornly resist assimilation. A few anomalies are tolerated, but when they multiply, strike at the paradigm's core, or block important work, confidence erodes and the field slips into crisis. In crisis, foundational assumptions are questioned and competing candidates emerge, until a new paradigm wins allegiance and a revolution occurs. Kuhn held that this transition is not a purely logical inference from neutral data, because rival paradigms are incommensurable: their key terms shift meaning, they disagree about which problems and standards matter, and their proponents in a sense see the world differently, a change Kuhn likened to a Gestalt switch, so that theory choice involves persuasion and judgment and is not compelled by an algorithm. After the revolution, a new period of normal science begins under the new paradigm.

examples.text: The shift from an Earth-centered to a Sun-centered cosmos is a classic paradigm shift in Kuhn's account.
Scientists puzzle-solve within a paradigm until accumulating anomalies trigger a crisis and a possible revolution.
Lavoisier's oxygen replaced the phlogiston theory; where Priestley saw dephlogisticated air, Lavoisier saw oxygen.

variants.name: Normal science versus revolution
variants.text: The contrast between routine puzzle-solving within a paradigm and the upheaval that replaces one paradigm with another.

whyItMatters: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions is one of the most influential books of the twentieth century, and paradigm shift has become one of the few pieces of philosophy of science to enter ordinary language. Kuhn challenged the received picture of science as a steady, cumulative march toward truth, arguing instead that scientific change is punctuated by revolutions in which whole frameworks are overturned and the world is, in a sense, reconceived. This reframing transformed the history and philosophy of science and rippled far beyond, into the social sciences, the humanities, and popular culture, where the language of paradigms and their shifts is now everywhere. His concepts, normal science, anomaly, crisis, revolution, incommensurability, and the exemplar, gave scholars a powerful vocabulary for describing how disciplines actually work. The account also provoked lasting controversy, since Kuhn's claim that theory choice is not fully determined by neutral evidence and logic led critics to charge him with relativism and irrationalism about science, a charge he resisted and his later work softened. Whether embraced or contested, Kuhn's picture reset the terms of debate about scientific progress, objectivity, and rationality. As the idea that science advances through revolutionary shifts of paradigm, it is a landmark of modern thought.

working.text: conduct normal science, solving puzzles that articulate and extend the shared framework.
encounter results the paradigm cannot explain, which build until the field enters crisis.
replace the old paradigm with a new one that reconceives the field, an incommensurable shift.

limits: Kuhn's account is powerful but heavily contested, and Kuhn himself refined it over time. The concept of a paradigm is notoriously slippery, used in many senses, which prompted Kuhn's later distinction between disciplinary matrix and exemplar and left room for very loose popular usage. The most serious philosophical objection concerns incommensurability and theory choice: if rival paradigms lack a neutral common measure and the choice between them is not compelled by evidence and logic, critics such as Karl Popper charged that Kuhn made science irrational or relativistic, a mob-psychology of conversion rather than reasoned progress. Kuhn firmly rejected the relativist label, insisting that incommensurable does not mean incomparable and that paradigm choice, though not algorithmic, is guided by shared values like accuracy, scope, and simplicity, and his later writings emphasized this. Historians have also questioned whether real episodes fit the tidy cycle of normal science, crisis, and revolution as neatly as the model suggests, and whether change is always so discontinuous. So paradigm shift robustly captures the revolutionary character of major scientific change, understood as an influential but contested model dogged by the ambiguity of paradigm and the charge of relativism about theory choice.
misreadings: A paradigm shift is not simply any change of opinion or minor advance; in Kuhn's sense it is a revolutionary replacement of one disciplinary framework by an incommensurable rival, preceded by anomaly and crisis. Incommensurability does not mean the paradigms are incomparable or that theory choice is arbitrary, a reading Kuhn rejected, since choice is still guided by shared scientific values. And Kuhn did not claim science is irrational, though critics pressed that charge, so treating any change as a paradigm shift, reading incommensurability as sheer relativism, or taking Kuhn to deny scientific rationality, misreads his account of scientific revolutions.
origin: Thomas Kuhn's account, in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), of scientific change as a cycle of normal science, anomaly, crisis, and revolutionary replacement of one incommensurable paradigm by another.

sources.text: Thomas Kuhn, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Kuhn's account of paradigms, normal science as puzzle-solving, anomaly and crisis leading to scientific revolutions and paradigm shifts, the disciplinary matrix and exemplar, incommensurability and the non-algorithmic character of theory choice, the Copernican, Newton-to-Einstein, and chemical revolutions, and Kuhn's rejection of the relativist charge.

Margaret Masterman, The Nature of a Paradigm, in Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970). — the identification of at least twenty-one different senses of paradigm in Kuhn's book, prompting his later refinements.
